title: Filing an FIR in Nepal
content: In Nepal, any person can file a First Information Report (FIR) at the nearest police station regarding a criminal offense. The police must register the FIR within 24 hours of receiving the complaint. You can file a written or verbal complaint. After registration, the police will investigate and file a charge sheet in court if sufficient evidence exists. You should keep a copy of the FIR for your records. If the police refuse to register your FIR, you can approach the Superintendent of Police or file a complaint directly to the court under Section 155 of the Criminal Procedure Code 2074.

title: Arrest and Bail Rights
content: Under the Constitution of Nepal and the Muluki Criminal Code 2017, any person arrested has the right to know the reason for arrest, right to consult a lawyer, and right against torture. The police must produce the arrested person before a judicial authority within 24 hours. Bail is a right for most bailable offenses. For non-bailable offenses, you can apply for bail from the court. The court considers the severity of the crime, evidence, and flight risk when granting bail. Repeated refusal of bail can be challenged in the High Court.

title: Domestic Violence Protection
content: Domestic Violence in Nepal is addressed under the Domestic Violence (Offense and Punishment) Act 2066. Victims can file complaints at the Women's Cell of any police station, or call the helpline 1145. Protection orders can be obtained from the court to prevent further violence. Medical certificates are crucial evidence. The law covers physical, mental, sexual, and economic abuse. The perpetrator may face imprisonment from 6 months to 2 years and fines. Free legal aid is available through the Nepal Legal Aid and Consultancy Center.

title: Theft and Robbery Legal Process
content: Theft (चोरी) and robbery (लुटपाट) are criminal offenses under the Muluki Criminal Code 2017. Theft involves taking someone's property without consent. Robbery involves taking property through force or threat. Immediate steps include filing an FIR at the nearest police station, preserving any CCTV footage, and listing stolen items with estimated values. The police investigate and file charges. Penalties vary from 1-7 years imprisonment depending on the severity and value of property stolen.

title: Cyber Crime and Online Fraud
content: Cyber crimes in Nepal are governed by the Electronic Transaction Act 2063. This covers hacking, identity theft, online fraud, cyber bullying, and unauthorized data access. Victims should immediately report to the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau at 01-4779900 or visit their office at Narayanhiti, Kathmandu. Save all evidence including screenshots, transaction records, emails, and chat logs. The law provides for imprisonment up to 5 years and fines up to NPR 200,000 for hacking offenses. Banking fraud should also be reported to Nepal Rastra Bank and your bank immediately.

title: Land Registration Process
content: Land registration in Nepal is done at the Land Revenue Office (Malpot Office) under the Land Revenue Act 2034. The process requires a deed of sale, citizenship certificate of both parties, land ownership certificate (Lalpurja), cadastral map, and photos. The registration fee is approximately 5% of the land value (4% for women to encourage female ownership). Both parties must be present. The entire process typically takes 1-7 days after submission. Registration provides legal ownership rights and is essential for any property transaction.

title: Property Dispute Resolution
content: Property disputes in Nepal can be resolved through several channels. First, attempt mediation at the local level through community elders or ward office. For registered land disputes, file a case at the District Court. The Land Revenue Office can resolve boundary disputes through survey. The Land Tribunal handles certain land-related cases faster. Common disputes include boundary encroachment, ownership claims, inheritance division, and fraudulent transactions. Always verify property documents at the Land Revenue Office before purchasing. Court cases can take 1-3 years for resolution.

title: Tenant and Landlord Rights
content: The relationship between tenants and landlords in Nepal is governed by the existing civil laws and contractual agreements. A written rental agreement is strongly recommended. Landlords must provide 6 months notice for eviction unless there is a breach of contract. Tenants must pay rent on time and maintain the property. Security deposits (typically 1-3 months rent) must be returned when the tenant vacates, minus legitimate deductions. Rent increases are negotiated between parties. Courts handle eviction cases if tenants refuse to vacate after proper notice.

title: Inheritance and Property Division
content: In Nepal, property inheritance is governed by the Muluki Ain (Civil Code) 2017. Sons and unmarried daughters have equal rights to ancestral property. Married daughters have rights to parental property if they are divorced, widowed, or separated. A person can create a will to distribute self-acquired property. Without a will, property is divided equally among legal heirs. The District Court handles inheritance disputes. Property acquired before marriage remains separate property. Married women have equal rights to property acquired during marriage.

title: Filing a Civil Lawsuit
content: Civil lawsuits in Nepal are filed at the District Court under the Civil Procedure Code 2074. The plaintiff files a petition stating the facts, legal grounds, and relief sought. Court fees are calculated based on the claim value (approximately 1-2% for monetary claims). The defendant must respond within 15-30 days of receiving notice. The court may order mediation before trial. Evidence is submitted including documents, witnesses, and expert opinions. The process from filing to judgment typically takes 6 months to 2 years. Appeals go to the High Court and then the Supreme Court.

title: Contract Law and Breach of Contract
content: Contract law in Nepal is governed by the Contract Act 2063. A valid contract requires offer, acceptance, consideration, and legal purpose. Contracts can be written or oral, but written contracts are strongly recommended for enforceability. If a contract is breached, the aggrieved party can send a legal notice demanding performance or compensation. If unresolved, a civil suit can be filed for damages. The limitation period for breach of contract is generally 2 years from the breach. Remedies include specific performance, damages, or contract termination.

title: Debt Recovery and Loan Disputes
content: For debt recovery in Nepal, the standard process begins with a formal demand letter to the debtor. If payment is not made within the specified time (usually 7-30 days), a civil suit can be filed at the District Court. Interest on loans is governed by the Nepal Rastra Bank directives. For loans with collateral, the creditor can seek attachment and auction of the collateral through court. The limitation period for debt recovery is 2 years from the date the debt becomes due. For microfinance and bank loans, there are special recovery procedures under the Banking Offenses Act.

title: Mediation and Alternative Dispute Resolution
content: Mediation is an alternative dispute resolution method encouraged by Nepali courts. The Mediation Act 2068 provides the legal framework. Mediation is voluntary, confidential, and less expensive than court litigation. Many courts require mediation before trial for civil cases. The mediator facilitates negotiations between parties. If settlement is reached, it is filed in court as a binding agreement. Mediation is particularly effective for family disputes, property division, contract disputes, and neighbor conflicts. The process typically takes 1-3 months compared to 1-2 years for court cases.

title: Company Registration in Nepal
content: Companies in Nepal are registered with the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR) under the Companies Act 2063. Types include Private Limited, Public Limited, and One Person Company. The process requires name approval, submission of MOA/AOA, details of directors and shareholders, and registered address. Private Limited companies need minimum 1 director and 1 shareholder (can be same person). Registration costs approximately NPR 20,000-50,000 including government fees. After registration, obtain PAN from the Tax Department, register for VAT if turnover exceeds NPR 50 lakh annually, and register with Social Security Fund.

title: Tax Compliance for Businesses
content: Businesses in Nepal must comply with the Income Tax Act 2058 and VAT Act 2052. Income tax is filed annually within 3 months of the fiscal year end (mid-July). VAT returns are filed quarterly (for businesses with turnover NPR 50 lakh-2 crore) or monthly (above 2 crore). TDS must be deducted and deposited monthly. Late filing attracts penalties of 5-20% of tax liability. Businesses must maintain proper books of accounts for 6 years. Tax audits are required for companies with turnover exceeding NPR 2 crore. PAN registration is mandatory for all businesses before starting operations.

title: Partnership and Shareholder Disputes
content: Partnership and shareholder disputes in Nepal are governed by the Companies Act 2063 and the Partnership Act. Common disputes include profit sharing disagreements, removal of directors, share transfer issues, and mismanagement. The first step is reviewing the partnership agreement or company bylaws. Mediation is recommended before litigation. Shareholders can file oppression and mismanagement petitions at the Company Registrar. Partnership disputes can be filed at the District Court. Deadlock provisions in the agreement can force dissolution or buyout. Legal costs vary based on complexity but typically range from NPR 100,000-500,000.

title: Business Licensing and Permits
content: Different businesses in Nepal require different licenses and permits. The Industrial Enterprises Act 2020 governs industrial licenses. Basic requirements include business registration certificate, PAN, and local municipality license. Specific businesses need additional permits: restaurants need food license from Department of Food Technology, construction companies need contractor license, pharmaceutical businesses need drug license, and financial services need Nepal Rastra Bank approval. Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is required for large industries. Operating without proper licenses can result in fines and closure. Most licenses must be renewed annually.

title: Marriage Registration and Requirements
content: Marriage in Nepal must be registered at the Municipal or Ward Office under the Marriage Registration Act 2028. Both parties must be at least 20 years old for marriage. Required documents include citizenship certificates, passport photos, and two witnesses. For inter-caste marriages, additional verification may be required but such marriages are legally valid. Registration provides legal recognition and is necessary for spousal benefits, visa applications, and inheritance rights. Foreign nationals must provide additional documentation including a certificate of no impediment. Same-sex marriages are not currently legally recognized in Nepal despite some court directions.

title: Divorce Process in Nepal
content: Divorce in Nepal can be obtained through mutual consent or contested proceedings. For mutual consent divorce, both parties file a joint petition at the District Court. The court grants divorce after a 3-month reconciliation period if reconciliation fails. For contested divorce, grounds include adultery, cruelty, desertion for 3+ years, mental illness, and mutual incompatibility. The divorce petition includes details of property division, child custody arrangements, and maintenance claims. The process takes 3-6 months for mutual consent and 6-18 months for contested divorce. Legal representation is strongly recommended.

title: Child Custody and Maintenance
content: Child custody in Nepal is determined based on the best interests of the child. For children under 5 years, custody is typically granted to the mother. For children above 5, the court considers the child's preference (especially for 10+ years), financial stability, and moral fitness of parents. Joint custody arrangements are becoming more common. Child maintenance is calculated based on the non-custodial parent's income and needs of the child. Typically 20-30% of income is ordered for one child, more for multiple children. Custody and maintenance orders can be modified if circumstances change significantly.

title: Dowry and Anti-Dowry Laws
content: Dowry is illegal in Nepal under the Social Practices Reform (Dowry) Act 2033. Giving, taking, or demanding dowry is a criminal offense punishable by imprisonment of up to 3 months and/or a fine. Despite the law, dowry practices continue in many communities. Victims of dowry harassment can file complaints at the Women's Cell of Nepal Police or the National Women Commission. The court can order protection and restitution. Family members who commit dowry-related violence face enhanced penalties. Education and awareness programs by NGOs have helped reduce dowry practices in urban areas.

title: Wills and Inheritance in Nepal
content: Under Nepali law, any person 18 years or older with sound mind can create a will (testament). The will should be in writing, signed by the testator, and witnessed by two persons. Registration at the District Court is recommended but not mandatory. Self-acquired property can be willed to anyone including non-family members. Ancestral property follows specific inheritance rules under the Muluki Ain. If someone dies without a will (intestate), the property is distributed among legal heirs according to law. Spouses, children, and parents are primary heirs. A will can be contested in court on grounds of fraud, undue influence, or unsound mind.

title: Employment Contract and Rights
content: The Labor Act 2017 governs employment relationships in Nepal. Employment contracts should specify salary, working hours, leave entitlements, and termination conditions. The minimum wage is NPR 17,300 per month (as of 2024) for general workers. Standard working hours are 8 hours per day and 48 hours per week. Overtime must be paid at 1.5 times the regular rate. Employees are entitled to 14 days annual leave, 12 days sick leave, and public holidays. Festival bonus of 8.33% of annual salary is mandatory. Employers must register employees with the Social Security Fund within 30 days of hiring.

title: Termination and Unfair Dismissal
content: Termination of employment in Nepal requires 30 days written notice or payment in lieu of notice. The employer must have valid grounds for termination including misconduct, poor performance, or redundancy. Unfair dismissal can be challenged at the Labor Court or High Court. Remedies include reinstatement or compensation (up to 3 months salary per year of service). Employees with 3+ years continuous service are entitled to gratuity (one month salary per year). Retrenchment compensation is available in case of business closure. Fixed-term contracts end automatically without additional compensation.

title: Social Security Fund and Provident Fund
content: The Social Security Fund (SSF) in Nepal provides social protection to formal sector employees. Both employer and employee contribute 10% each of basic salary (total 20%) to the fund. Contributions cover medical, health, and maternity benefits, accident and disability insurance, dependent family benefits, and old age protection. Provident Fund (PF) is separate and typically handled by individual companies. On employment termination, employees can withdraw their PF and SSF contributions with applicable interest. The SSF is managed by the Social Security Fund Office under the Ministry of Labor.

title: Workplace Harassment and Discrimination
content: Workplace harassment, including sexual harassment, is prohibited under the Labor Act 2017. Employers must maintain a safe working environment and have anti-harassment policies. Victims can file complaints with the employer's internal committee or directly at the Labor Office. Sexual harassment carries penalties including termination for the perpetrator. Discrimination based on gender, caste, religion, or disability is illegal. Women are entitled to 14 weeks paid maternity leave (before and after childbirth). Paternity leave of 15 days is available. The Labor Court handles harassment claims and can award compensation.

title: Nepal Citizenship Process
content: Nepal citizenship is governed by the Nepal Citizenship Act 2063. Citizenship is acquired by birth (born to Nepali parents), descent (born abroad to Nepali parents), or naturalization (15+ years residence). The application is submitted at the District Administration Office (DAO) with required documents including birth certificate, parent's citizenship, and residence proof. The process takes 30-90 days. Non-Resident Nepali (NRN) citizenship is available for former Nepali citizens who have adopted foreign citizenship, providing special economic and visa benefits. Dual citizenship is not fully implemented for ordinary citizens.

title: Passport Application in Nepal
content: Nepali passports are issued by the Department of Passports under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Applications are submitted online through the passport portal and then visit the designated passport office for biometric collection. Required documents include citizenship certificate, previous passport (if renewal), and application fee. Regular passport processing takes 15-30 days. Expedited processing (1-7 days) is available for urgent cases with additional fees. Passport offices are located in Kathmandu, Birgunj, Nepalgunj, Pokhara, and other major cities. Machine Readable Passports (MRP) are the current standard with 5 or 10-year validity.

title: Visa Types and Extension
content: Nepal offers various visa types: tourist visa (30/90/150 days), business visa, student visa, work visa, and dependent visa. Tourist visas can be obtained on arrival at Kathmandu airport or land borders. Tourist visa costs: USD 30 for 15 days, USD 50 for 30 days, USD 125 for 90 days. Visa extensions are available from the Department of Immigration, Kalikasthan, Kathmandu. For long-term stays, work and student visas require sponsorship from a Nepali entity. Overstaying fines are USD 5 per day for first 30 days, USD 2 per day thereafter. Employment without a work visa is illegal.

title: Foreign Employment Law
content: The Foreign Employment Act 2076 governs Nepali citizens working abroad. Licensed recruitment agencies must process foreign employment. Workers must obtain work permits from the Department of Foreign Employment before leaving Nepal. The minimum age for foreign employment is 18 years. Free visa and free ticket policy applies for some destination countries. Workers have rights to the terms specified in their employment contract. Insurance coverage of NPR 1,000,000 (life) and NPR 700,000 (accident) is mandatory. Welfare funds provide support in emergencies. Destination countries include UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Malaysia, Kuwait, and South Korea.

title: Consumer Rights and Protection
content: The Consumer Protection Act 2075 provides comprehensive consumer rights in Nepal. Consumers have the right to safe products, accurate information, fair pricing, and redress. Defective products can be returned or exchanged within 7 days of purchase. Complaints can be filed at the Consumer Protection Department, district consumer forums, or directly at the Department of Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection. The law prohibits overcharging, misleading advertisements, and selling expired goods. Penalties for violations include fines up to NPR 500,000 and imprisonment. The consumer helpline number is 01-4220123.

title: Online Shopping and E-Commerce Rights
content: Online shopping in Nepal is regulated under the Electronic Transaction Act 2063 and Consumer Protection Act. Consumers have the right to cancel online orders within 48 hours of purchase. Products must be delivered within the promised timeframe. If goods are damaged or not as described, consumers can demand replacement or refund. Payment security is the responsibility of the e-commerce platform. Fraudulent online stores should be reported to the Cyber Bureau. Keep screenshots of orders, payment confirmations, and communication with sellers. Cross-border online purchases may be subject to customs duties.

title: Defective Products and Warranty Claims
content: In Nepal, consumer goods come with implied warranties under the Consumer Protection Act. Manufacturers and sellers must provide after-sales service. Warranty periods vary by product: electronics typically 1 year, vehicles 3 years or 100,000 km. For warranty claims, keep the original purchase receipt, warranty card, and product packaging. The seller must repair or replace defective products within a reasonable time. If the same defect appears multiple times, the consumer can demand a full refund. Importers are also responsible for warranty on imported goods. File complaints at the Department of Commerce if the seller refuses.

title: Fundamental Rights under Constitution
content: The Constitution of Nepal 2015 guarantees 31 fundamental rights including right to equality (Article 18), right to freedom (Article 17), right to justice (Article 20), right to property (Article 25), right to information (Article 27), and right to constitutional remedies (Article 46). These rights are enforceable in the Supreme Court through writ petitions. The right to life includes clean environment, food, and shelter. Discrimination on grounds of origin, religion, race, caste, sex, or physical condition is prohibited. Special provisions exist for women, children, Dalits, indigenous groups, and persons with disabilities.

title: Right to Information (RTI)
content: The Right to Information Act 2064 (RTI) gives Nepali citizens the right to access information held by public bodies. File an application with the concerned public office. The office must respond within 15 days. If information is denied or delayed, appeal to the Information Commission within 60 days. Information can be denied only on grounds of national security, court confidentiality, or personal privacy. The RTI covers all government ministries, departments, local bodies, and public corporations. The National Information Commission oversees RTI compliance and can impose fines on officers who refuse information without valid reason.

title: Writ Jurisdiction and Supreme Court
content: The Supreme Court of Nepal has extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 133 of the Constitution to issue writs including habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, and quo warranto. Habeas corpus is for unlawful detention. Mandamus orders a public body to perform its duty. Certiorari quashes illegal decisions. Prohibition prevents tribunals from exceeding jurisdiction. Quo warranto challenges unlawful holding of public office. Writ petitions must be filed within 35 days of the cause of action. Constitutional bench of the Supreme Court hears cases involving constitutional interpretation. Free legal aid is available for indigent petitioners through the Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee.

title: Driving License in Nepal
content: Driving licenses in Nepal are issued by the Department of Transport Management (DOTM). Minimum age is 18 for motorcycles (15-30 cc) and 21 for cars and heavy vehicles. The process includes written exam, driving test, and trail test (for public vehicles). Required documents include citizenship certificate, medical certificate, and photos. Training from a licensed driving center is recommended but not mandatory. The license is valid for 5 years and must be renewed. Fees range from NPR 1,200-3,600 depending on vehicle category. International Driving Permit (IDP) can be obtained for overseas driving.

title: Vehicle Registration and Insurance
content: All vehicles in Nepal must be registered with the Department of Transport Management within 30 days of purchase. Required documents include purchase invoice, customs receipt (for imports), citizenship, and VAT receipt. Number plates must be displayed. Vehicle tax is paid annually. Third-party insurance is mandatory by law and covers damage to others. Comprehensive insurance covers own vehicle damage. Insurance claims must be filed within 30 days of an accident. Uninsured vehicles face fines and possible seizure. Registration renewal requires passing a fitness test for vehicles older than 5 years.

title: Road Accidents and Compensation
content: In case of a road accident in Nepal, immediately report to the nearest traffic police or call 103. Ensure medical treatment for injured persons. File an FIR at the police station. The traffic police investigate and determine fault. Insurance companies process claims based on the police report and medical documents. Compensation for injury includes medical expenses, loss of income, and pain and suffering. In case of death, dependents can claim compensation up to NPR 1,000,000 from insurance. Legal action can be taken against the at-fault driver under the Transport Management Act. Hit-and-run cases are investigated by dedicated traffic police units.

title: Income Tax Filing and Slabs
content: Income tax in Nepal is governed by the Income Tax Act 2058. The tax year runs from mid-July to mid-July. Tax returns must be filed by October 15 (3 months after fiscal year end). Current tax slabs for individuals: Up to NPR 5,00,000 - 1%, NPR 5,00,001 to 7,00,000 - 10%, NPR 7,00,001 to 10,00,000 - 20%, NPR 10,00,001 to 20,00,000 - 30%, Above 20,00,000 - 36%. Married couples filing jointly get additional NPR 50,000 deduction. Tax is deducted at source (TDS) for salary, rent, and certain payments. Late filing attracts penalties and interest of 15% per annum.

title: VAT Registration and Compliance
content: Value Added Tax (VAT) in Nepal is at 13% standard rate. Businesses with annual turnover exceeding NPR 50 lakh must register for VAT. Registration is done at the Inland Revenue Department (IRD). VAT returns are filed quarterly (turnover 50 lakh - 2 crore) or monthly (above 2 crore). Input tax credit is available for business purchases. VAT invoices must include business name, PAN, VAT number, and tax amount. Zero-rated supplies (exports) and exempt supplies (agricultural products, education, health services) have special rules. Penalties for non-compliance range from 25% to 200% of tax evaded.

title: Tax Audit and Disputes
content: Tax audits in Nepal are conducted by the Inland Revenue Department (IRD). Companies with turnover exceeding NPR 2 crore must submit audited financial statements. The IRD can audit returns within 4 years of filing. During an audit, taxpayers must provide books of accounts, invoices, bank statements, and contracts. Tax disputes can be appealed to the Revenue Tribunal within 30 days of the assessment order. Further appeal goes to the Supreme Court. Tax amnesty schemes periodically offer reduced penalties for voluntary disclosure. Professional tax representation is recommended for complex audits.

title: Free Legal Aid in Nepal
content: Free legal aid is available in Nepal for indigent persons through the Nepal Legal Aid and Consultancy Center (NLACC) under the Supreme Court. Legal aid covers consultation, representation in court, and document preparation. Eligibility is based on income (below poverty line) and case merit. Legal aid clinics operate in all District Courts. The Nepal Bar Association also provides pro bono services through its legal aid committee. Organizations like Pro Public and Forum for Women, Law and Development (FWLD) provide specialized legal aid for women and marginalized groups. Free legal advice is also available at court premises.

title: Drug Offenses and NDPS Act
content: Drug offenses in Nepal are governed by the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act 2033. Possession, use, sale, or trafficking of controlled substances is illegal. Penalties vary by drug type and quantity: possession for personal use may result in rehabilitation, while trafficking carries 5-20 years imprisonment and fines up to NPR 1,000,000. Common drugs include cannabis, heroin, cocaine, and prescription drug abuse. The police have special narcotics control bureaus. First-time offenders may be offered rehabilitation instead of prosecution for small quantities. International drug trafficking carries the highest penalties.

title: Defamation and Libel Law
content: Defamation in Nepal is a both civil and criminal offense. Under the Muluki Criminal Code 2017, defamation occurs when false statements harm a person's reputation. Criminal defamation carries penalties of up to 1 year imprisonment or fine. Civil defamation requires proving that false statements were published to third parties and caused damage. Defenses include truth, fair comment on public figures, and privilege. Social media defamation is increasingly common and is addressed under the Electronic Transaction Act. Public figures must prove actual malice to win defamation cases. Written defamation (libel) is considered more serious than spoken (slander).

title: Trade Union and Collective Bargaining
content: Workers in Nepal have the right to form and join trade unions under the Labor Act 2017. Trade unions can engage in collective bargaining with employers on wages, working conditions, and benefits. There must be at least 10 workers to form a union. Unions are registered with the Department of Labor. Strikes are legal after following prescribed procedures including notice to the employer and mandatory conciliation. Essential services have restrictions on strikes. Employers cannot discriminate against union members. The Labor Court handles disputes between unions and employers.

title: Adoption Laws in Nepal
content: Adoption in Nepal is governed by the Muluki Ain and the Child Adoption Guidelines 2065. Adoption can be domestic (within Nepal) or inter-country. Eligible adoptive parents must be 25+ years old and at least 18 years older than the child. Married couples must have spousal consent. Single women can adopt, single men cannot adopt female children. The process involves home study, counseling, and court approval. The Central Child Welfare Board oversees adoptions. Inter-country adoption follows the Hague Convention principles. Birth parents must give free and informed consent. Adopted children have the same inheritance rights as biological children.

title: Sexual Assault and Rape Laws
content: Sexual assault and rape are serious criminal offenses under the Muluki Criminal Code 2017. Rape carries 10-15 years imprisonment and up to life imprisonment for aggravated cases (child victim, multiple perpetrators, or causing death). The law recognizes marital rape (except when spouses are living separately). Victims must undergo medical examination at a government hospital within 24 hours. FIR should be filed at any police station. Victim identity is protected by law. Special provisions include in-camera proceedings and female-only investigation officers. Support services are available through the One-Stop Crisis Management Center at major government hospitals.

title: Intellectual Property Rights
content: Intellectual Property (IP) in Nepal is protected under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act 2022. Trademarks protect brand names, logos, and slogans. Registration is with the Department of Industry, Industrial Property Office. Trademark protection lasts 7 years and is renewable. Patents protect inventions for 20 years. Copyright protection under the Copyright Act 2058 covers literary, artistic, and musical works automatically upon creation (registration not required but recommended). Nepal is a member of WTO and Paris Convention for IP protection. IP infringement can be addressed through court injunctions, damages, and criminal penalties.

title: Banking and Financial Fraud
content: Banking fraud in Nepal is addressed under the Banking Offenses Act 2064 and Nepal Rastra Bank directives. Common frauds include unauthorized transactions, loan fraud, kiting, and identity theft. Victims must immediately notify their bank and file a complaint with Nepal Rastra Bank. Bank fraud investigation is conducted by the Nepal Police Economic Crime Investigation Department. Electronic banking fraud should also be reported to the Cyber Bureau. Banks must reimburse unauthorized transactions if reported within 3 days. Loan fraud carries 3-10 years imprisonment. The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation provides deposit insurance up to NPR 500,000 per depositor.

title: Housing and Apartment Buyer Rights
content: Apartment and housing buyers in Nepal have rights under the Land Use Act 2076 and Real Estate Development Guidelines. Developers must register with the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction. Buyers should verify that the developer has clear land title and building permit. The agreement must specify delivery date, specifications, payment schedule, and penalty for delays. If the developer fails to deliver, buyers can demand refund with interest (typically 10-12% per annum). Common issues include delayed possession, substandard construction, and unauthorized floor area. File complaints at the Department of Commerce or the District Court.

title: Insurance Claims and Disputes
content: Insurance claims in Nepal are governed by the Insurance Act 2079. Policyholders must file claims with all supporting documents within the policy period. Life insurance claims are processed within 30 days of receiving all documents. Non-life claims (motor, health, property) are processed within 15 days for cashless and 30 days for reimbursement. If the insurer rejects or delays claims unreasonably, policyholders can complain to the Insurance Board of Nepal (Beema Samiti). The Beema Samiti can order the insurer to pay with 12% interest. For complex disputes, consumers can file suit at the District Court. Complaint hotline: 01-4412549.

title: Environmental Law and Rights
content: The Constitution of Nepal guarantees the right to a clean environment (Article 30). The Environment Protection Act 2076 governs environmental protection. Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is mandatory for development projects. Initial Environmental Examination (IEE) is required for smaller projects. Citizens can file cases in the Supreme Court against projects that harm the environment. Polluters face fines up to NPR 500,000 and imprisonment. The National Trust for Nature Conservation manages protected areas. Solid waste management is regulated by the Solid Waste Management Act 2068. Community forestry programs give local communities forest management rights.

title: Juvenile Justice and Children's Rights
content: The Children's Act 2075 and Juvenile Justice Procedure Rules protect children in conflict with the law. Children below 10 years cannot be held criminally responsible. Children 10-18 years have special procedures including separate detention facilities, closed hearings, and alternative sentencing. The Juvenile Bench in District Courts handles juvenile cases. Rehabilitation, not punishment, is the primary goal. Reform homes and child correction homes provide rehabilitation. Parents or guardians are responsible for damages caused by children. Child labor below 14 years is prohibited. Children have the right to education, health, and protection from exploitation under the Constitution.

title: Citizen Charter and Public Service Rights
content: Public service offices in Nepal are required to publish Citizen Charters specifying services, response times, fees, and grievance mechanisms. The Citizen Charter must be displayed prominently at every public office. If a service is not provided within the specified time, the concerned officer must compensate the citizen. The Grievance Handling Act 2075 provides for filing complaints against public officials. Complaints can be filed at the office itself, the Ministry, or the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA). The CIAA investigates corruption and abuse of authority. Citizen awareness of these rights is essential for accountable governance.

title: Constitution of Nepal 2015 - Overview and Structure
content: The Constitution of Nepal 2015 (Nepal Sashan Bidhan 2072) is the supreme law of Nepal, enacted on September 20, 2015. It replaced the Interim Constitution of 2007. The Constitution establishes Nepal as a federal democratic republic with seven provinces. It consists of 35 parts, 308 articles, and 9 schedules. The Constitution guarantees sovereignty vested in the Nepali people. Key features include constitutional supremacy, fundamental rights, three levels of government (federal, provincial, local), independent judiciary, and an inclusive electoral system. The Constitution can be amended by a two-thirds majority of both houses of the federal parliament.

title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Nepal
content: Part 3 (Articles 16-46) of the Constitution of Nepal 2015 guarantees comprehensive fundamental rights enforceable in the Supreme Court. These include: Right to life (Article 16), Right to dignity (Article 16), Right to freedom (Article 17), Right to equality (Article 18), Right to communication (Article 19), Right to justice (Article 20), Right of a victim of crime (Article 21), Right against torture (Article 22), Right against preventive detention (Article 23), Right against untouchability and discrimination (Article 24), Right to education (Article 31), Right to language and culture (Article 32), Right to employment and social security (Article 33-34), Right to health (Article 35), Right to food (Article 36), Right to housing (Article 37), Right to a clean environment (Article 30), Right to information (Article 27), and Right to constitutional remedies (Article 46). Any law inconsistent with fundamental rights is void.

title: Federal Structure of Nepal - Three Levels of Government
content: The Constitution establishes three levels of government: Federal (Sanghiya), Provincial (Pradesh), and Local (Sthaniya). The Federal level consists of the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister, Council of Ministers, and the Federal Parliament (House of Representatives and National Assembly). The 7 provinces each have a Provincial Assembly and Chief Minister. The 753 local levels include Metropolitan cities, Sub-Metropolitan cities, Municipalities, and Rural Municipalities (Gaunpalika). Schedule 5-9 of the Constitution define the powers and responsibilities of each level. The federal government handles defense, foreign affairs, central banking, and national infrastructure. Provincial governments handle provincial police, health, and education. Local governments handle local development, agriculture, and community services.

title: Supreme Court and Judicial System of Nepal
content: The judicial system of Nepal comprises the Supreme Court, seven High Courts (one per province), and 77 District Courts. The Supreme Court is the highest court with final appellate jurisdiction and extraordinary constitutional jurisdiction through writ petitions (habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, and quo warranto). The Chief Justice heads the Supreme Court. The Judicial Council recommends appointments and oversees judicial conduct. The Judicial Service Commission handles promotions. The Constitutional Bench of the Supreme Court hears constitutional disputes. Specialized courts include Administrative Court, Revenue Tribunal, Debt Recovery Tribunal, Labor Court, and Special Court for corruption cases. Lower courts include the Juvenile Bench and the Court of Appeal at the District level.

title: Muluki Criminal Code 2017 - Key Provisions
content: The Muluki Criminal Code (Muluki Aparadh Sanhita) 2074 came into effect on August 17, 2018, replacing the old Muluki Ain. It contains 299 sections covering criminal offenses and punishments. Key offenses include murder (Section 173 - life imprisonment), attempted murder, culpable homicide, assault, kidnapping, rape (Section 219 - 10-15 years imprisonment), theft (Section 249 - up to 7 years), robbery (Section 253), dacoity, fraud (Section 259 - up to 7 years), defamation (Section 269), and perjury. The Code recognizes both acts and omissions as criminal. Attempt to commit an offense is punishable with half the maximum punishment. The principle of nulla poena sine lege (no punishment without law) is followed. Corporate criminal liability is recognized.

title: Criminal Procedure Code 2074 - Court Process
content: The Criminal Procedure Code (Muluki Aparadh Karobari Sanhita) 2074 governs criminal procedure in Nepal. It covers investigation, arrest, bail, trial, and appeal. The criminal process begins with FIR registration (Jahari), police investigation, filing of charge sheet (Abhiyog Patra), preliminary hearing, trial (full bench or jury), and judgment. Types of trials include summary trial for minor offenses, warrant trial for serious offenses, and sessions trial for capital offenses. Limitation periods: 6 months for summary offenses, 1 year for warrant offenses, and no limitation for serious crimes like murder. Appeal lies to the High Court within 70 days from the District Court judgment. Further appeal to the Supreme Court requires leave.

title: Civil Procedure Code 2074 - Civil Litigation
content: The Civil Procedure Code (Muluki Dewani Karobari Sanhita) 2074 governs civil litigation including property disputes, contract enforcement, and tort claims. A civil suit begins with filing a plaint at the District Court with court fees based on the claim amount. The court issues summons to the defendant who must file a written statement within 15-35 days. The court holds a preliminary hearing to frame issues, followed by evidence (documentary and witness), argument, and judgment. Mediation and settlement are encouraged at any stage. Limitation periods: 6 months for movable property recovery, 1 year for breach of contract, 3 years for immovable property, and 12 years for adverse possession. Appeals must be filed within 90 days to the High Court.

title: Marriage Laws in Nepal
content: Marriage in Nepal is governed by the Muluki Civil Code 2074. The legal marriage age is 20 years for both men and women. Marriage registration is mandatory and must be done within 35 days at the Ward Office or District Administration Office. Types of marriage include court marriage, religious marriage, and traditional marriage. Inter-caste marriage is legally recognized and incentivized with a NPR 100,000 cash incentive from the government. Polygamy is prohibited for all except under specific circumstances (first wife's consent for infertility or incurable disease). Dowry is illegal under the Social Practices Reform Act. Marriages must be voluntarily consented. Child marriage (below 20) is a criminal offense.

title: Divorce and Legal Separation in Nepal
content: Divorce in Nepal is governed by the Muluki Civil Code 2074. A divorce petition can be filed in the District Court. Grounds for divorce include mutual consent, cruelty, adultery, desertion for 3+ years, irreconcilable differences, and incurable mental illness. Mutual consent divorce requires both parties to file jointly. After divorce, the wife is entitled to half of the property acquired during marriage (not ancestral property). Child custody is determined based on the child's best interest. Children under 5 years are usually with the mother. Maintenance (alimony) is determined based on the spouse's income and standard of living. The court attempts mediation first. A 6-month cooling-off period is required for mutual consent divorce.

title: Succession and Inheritance Rights in Nepal
content: Succession in Nepal is governed by the Muluki Civil Code 2074. The law provides equal inheritance rights to sons and daughters. Ancestral property (Kulani) is divided equally among children. Self-acquired property can be disposed by will to anyone. The surviving spouse inherits a share equal to the children. If there is no will, property is distributed according to the rules of intestate succession. Stepchildren adopted under Nepali law have inheritance rights equal to biological children. A will (Vasiyathnama) should be registered at the District Court or signed by two witnesses. Testamentary succession allows a person to distribute their property according to their wishes. Women's right to parental property is fully protected under Article 18 of the Constitution.

title: Adoption Laws in Nepal
content: Adoption in Nepal is governed by the Muluki Civil Code 2074 and the Children's Act 2075. Both domestic and inter-country adoption are regulated. Domestic adoption: a married couple can adopt if they have no children of their own. Single women can adopt a female child. Foreign adoption is handled through authorized organizations. The adoptive parents must be at least 30 years old and at most 55 years old, financially stable, and of good character. The adopted child has the same inheritance rights as a biological child. The adoption must be registered at the District Administration Office. The consent of biological parents (if living) and the child (if above 10 years) is required. Abandoned children can be adopted through the Child Welfare Board.

title: Labor Act 2017 - Employee Rights
content: The Labor Act 2074 (2017) is the primary law governing employment in Nepal. Key provisions: Maximum 8 hours work per day (48 hours per week), overtime paid at 1.5 times regular pay, 20 days annual leave, 13 days public holiday leave, 12 days sick leave, 60 days maternity leave (fully paid), and 15 days paternity leave for male employees. Employees cannot be terminated without 30 days' notice or payment in lieu. Severance includes gratuity (8.33% of salary per year) and provident fund (10% employee + 10% employer). Minimum wage is set by the government and revised periodically. Employers must provide safe working conditions, accident insurance, and social security contributions. The Labor Office handles employee complaints.

title: Social Security Act - Employee Benefits
content: The Social Security Act 2075 established the Social Security Fund (SSF) for formal sector employees. Both employer and employee contribute 10% each of basic salary to the SSF. The SSF provides five schemes: Medical, Health and Maternity Protection Scheme; Accidents and Disability Protection Scheme; Dependent Family Protection Scheme; Old Age Protection Scheme; and Unemployment Protection Scheme. Registration is mandatory for all employers with employees. Unregistered employers face fines. The SSF is managed by the Social Security Fund Board. Employees can withdraw a portion of their old age contributions after age 60 or in case of permanent disability. The scheme also provides accident insurance coverage during employment.

title: Termination and Redundancy in Nepal
content: Employment termination in Nepal is regulated by the Labor Act 2074. Permanent employees can only be terminated for cause (misconduct, negligence, criminal offense) or redundancy (retrenchment). For-cause termination requires three written warnings within a year followed by a domestic inquiry. Redundancy requires the employer to prove economic necessity and follow a last-in-first-out principle. Notice period: 30 days for monthly employees, 7 days for daily wages. Severance pay: 30 days' basic salary per year of service as gratuity plus provident fund. Retrenched employees get additional compensation of 1 month salary per year of service (minimum 3 months, maximum 12 months). Wrongful termination can be challenged at the Labor Court, which can order reinstatement or compensation up to 36 months salary.

title: Personal Income Tax in Nepal
content: Personal income tax in Nepal is governed by the Income Tax Act 2058. The tax year runs from mid-July to mid-July (Nepali fiscal year). Tax rates (2024/25): Income up to NPR 500,000 - 1% (with social security contribution), NPR 500,001 to NPR 700,000 - 10%, NPR 700,001 to NPR 1,000,000 - 20%, NPR 1,000,001 to NPR 2,000,000 - 30%, above NPR 2,000,000 - 36%. Taxpayers with professional income (business, investment capital) get a 50% deduction on first NPR 500,000. Married couples can file separately. Tax is deducted at source (TDS) from salaries. Individuals must file annual tax returns by Kartik end (November) with penalties for late filing. Capital gains tax: 5% for shares (short-term), 7.5% for immovable property held less than 5 years.

title: Business and VAT Registration in Nepal
content: Business registration in Nepal is required at the Department of Commerce (Company) or Department of Cottage and Small Industries. VAT registration is mandatory for businesses with annual turnover exceeding NPR 5 million. Voluntary registration is allowed for smaller businesses. VAT rate is 13% on most goods and services (standard rate). Zero-rated supplies include exports, certain agricultural products, and services. VAT returns must be filed monthly (by 25th of following month). Late filing penalty is 2% per month with minimum NPR 1,000. PAN (Permanent Account Number) registration is required for all businesses. Advance Tax Payment (estimated tax) is payable in four installments during the fiscal year. Corporate tax rate: 25% for most businesses, 20% for industrial sectors, 10% for export businesses.

title: Land Measurement Units and Survey in Nepal
content: Land in Nepal is measured in traditional units: Ropani, Aana, Paisa, Daam (1 Ropani = 16 Aana = 508.72 sq meters) used in hilly regions, and Bigha, Kattha, Dhur (1 Bigha = 20 Kattha = 6772.41 sq meters) used in Terai. Land survey is conducted by the Survey Department. A cadastral survey creates the land map (Naksa) showing exact boundaries. The Land Revenue Office issues the Lalpurja (land ownership certificate). Land measurement disputes can be resolved through re-survey application. Land classification categories include: Aabbal, Doyam, Sim, Chahar (based on productivity). Land use classification under the Land Use Act: agricultural, residential, commercial, industrial, forest, and public use. Conversion of agricultural land to other uses requires approval from the Land Use Council.

title: Land Acquisition and Compensation
content: Land acquisition by the government is governed by the Land Acquisition Act 2034. The government can acquire private land for public purposes (infrastructure, roads, schools, hospitals). The acquisition process: publication of notice, survey and valuation, compensation determination, objection hearing, and final award. Compensation is based on market value plus 50% solatium. Displaced persons get additional rehabilitation allowance. If the acquired land is not used for the stated purpose within 5 years, the original owner has the right to recover it at the same price. Objections to compensation can be filed at the District Court. Landowners cannot refuse acquisition but can contest the compensation amount. The Land Acquisition Act Amendment 2069 increased compensation rates.

title: Contract Law in Nepal
content: Contracts in Nepal are governed by the Muluki Civil Code 2074 (Chapter on Contract). Essential elements of a valid contract: offer and acceptance, lawful consideration, capacity to contract (age 18+, sound mind), free consent, lawful object, and certainty of terms. Written contracts with registration are preferred for legal enforceability. Performance of contract must be as per agreed terms. Breach of contract remedies include specific performance, damages (actual loss + consequential loss), and rescission. Interest on delayed payment is 10% per annum unless otherwise agreed. Limitation for contract enforcement is 1 year from breach. Contracts involving immovable property must be registered at the Land Revenue Office. Unregistered contracts for immovable property are not enforceable in court.

title: Company Registration in Nepal
content: Companies in Nepal are registered under the Companies Act 2063 at the Office of Company Registrar (OCR), Tripureshwar, Kathmandu. Types: Private Limited Company (minimum 1 director, up to 101 shareholders), Public Limited Company (minimum 3 directors, 7+ shareholders, public can buy shares), and One Person Company (OPC). Registration process: Name reservation (online), document submission (MOA, AOA, etc.), incorporation certificate, PAN registration, and VAT registration. Minimum paid-up capital: Private Limited NPR 100,000, Public Limited NPR 10 million, OPC NPR 50,000. Foreign investment companies need approval from the Department of Industry. Annual requirements: AGM within 6 months of fiscal year end, annual return filing, and tax return. Non-compliance leads to fines and potential strike-off.

title: Passport and Citizenship in Nepal
content: Nepali passports are issued by the Department of Passports under the Passport Act 2076. Machine Readable Passports (MRP) are valid for 10 years. Application is online through the Department of Passports website with appointment booking. Required documents: citizenship certificate, birth certificate, and photographs. Emergency passport is available for urgent medical treatment and foreign employment. Citizenship in Nepal is governed by the Citizenship Act 2063. Citizenship by descent: persons born to Nepali citizen parents. Citizenship by birth: persons born in Nepal before 1990. Naturalized citizenship: available to foreign women married to Nepali citizens (after 7 years residence) and others with special contribution. Dual citizenship is not recognized. Non-Resident Nepali (NRN) status allows visa-free entry and economic rights without political rights.

title: Consumer Rights and Protection in Nepal
content: Consumer rights in Nepal are protected under the Consumer Protection Act 2075. The act provides for: right to safety, right to information, right to choose, right to be heard, and right to redress. The Department of Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection (DoCSCP) handles consumer complaints. Grievances can be filed through the toll-free number 1136 or online portal. Compensation for defective products: up to NPR 50,000 per complaint without court, and higher amounts through the Consumer Court. Black marketing, hoarding, and overcharging are punishable with imprisonment up to 10 years and fines up to NPR 300,000. Traders must display prices and expiry dates. Substandard products can be confiscated and destroyed. Right to return goods within 7 days is recognized for online purchases.

title: Driving License and Traffic Rules in Nepal
content: Driving licenses in Nepal are issued by the Department of Transport Management (DoTM). Categories: A (Motorcycle), B (Car/Taxi), C (Light Truck), D (Heavy Truck), E (Bus/Heavy Vehicle). Minimum age: 16 for motorcycle, 18 for car. Written test followed by driving test. License is valid for 5 years (renewable). Traffic rules: Left-hand drive, speed limits (40 km/h in cities, 80 km/h on highways), seat belts mandatory for front seats, helmet mandatory for motorcycle riders and pillion, no mobile phone while driving, zero tolerance for drunk driving (blood alcohol > 80mg/100ml is offense). Traffic violation fines range from NPR 500 to NPR 5,000. Accident procedures: Stop, help injured, inform police (100), inform insurance company, do not move vehicles until police arrive.

title: Human Rights and National Human Rights Commission
content: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) Nepal was established under the Human Rights Commission Act 2053. It is an independent constitutional body under Article 248 of the Constitution. Functions: investigate human rights violations, recommend compensation, visit detention centers, and recommend legal reforms. Complaints can be filed at NHRC offices in Kathmandu (Harihar Bhawan) and all provincial offices. The NHRC can summon officials, order investigations, and recommend action. However, its recommendations are not automatically enforceable. Victims can file cases in court based on NHRC findings. The NHRC has special procedures for women's rights, children's rights, and the rights of marginalized groups. Key rights protected: right against torture, right against enforced disappearance, right to fair trial, and freedom from discrimination.

title: Right to Information in Nepal
content: The Right to Information Act 2064 (2007) gives every citizen the right to access information held by public bodies. The National Information Commission (NIC) oversees implementation. Citizens can file information requests at any public office. The office must provide information within 15 days (3 days for matters involving life or liberty). Rejection requires written reasons (national security, privacy, ongoing investigation). If denied, appeal to the National Information Commission within 60 days. The Commission can impose fines up to NPR 25,000 and order the release of information. Annual reporting by all public bodies on proactive disclosure is mandatory. Public bodies must publish manuals, citizen charters, annual reports, and budgets proactively. The RTI Act has significantly increased government transparency in Nepal.

title: Education Rights and Law in Nepal
content: The right to education is a fundamental right under Article 31 of the Constitution. The Education Act 2028 governs the education system. Free and compulsory basic education (Grade 1-8) for all citizens is guaranteed. The government provides free textbooks and scholarships to marginalized students. The School Leaving Certificate (SEE) exam is conducted at Grade 10. Higher education is governed by the universities and their affiliated colleges. Key universities: Tribhuvan University, Kathmandu University, Pokhara University, Purbanchal University, and Nepal Sanskrit University. The University Grants Commission (UGC) funds and regulates higher education. Technical and vocational education is under the Council for Technical Education and Vocational Training (CTEVT). Private schools must be registered with the Ministry of Education and cannot charge fees arbitrarily.

title: Health Rights and Public Health Law in Nepal
content: The right to health is guaranteed under Article 35 of the Constitution. Every citizen has the right to free basic health services from government health facilities. The Public Health Service Act 2075 governs health service delivery. The Health Insurance Board operates the National Health Insurance Program providing health coverage for NPR 3,500 per family (5 members) per year with coverage up to NPR 100,000. Essential medicines are provided free at government hospitals. The Nepal Medical Council regulates doctors, Nepal Nursing Council regulates nurses, and the Nepal Health Professional Council regulates other health professionals. Medical malpractice liability is established under the Muluki Civil Code. Patients can file complaints with the Health Professional Councils. Government health facilities must provide emergency services free of charge.

title: Forest and Wildlife Protection Laws
content: Forest management in Nepal is governed by the Forest Act 2049 and the Forest Regulation 2051. The Community Forestry program gives local user groups management rights over forest areas. Nepal has 6 national parks, 12 wildlife reserves, and 10 conservation areas covering 24% of land. The National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act 2029 protects endangered species. Poaching penalties: 5-15 years imprisonment and fines up to NPR 1 million. Protected animals include the Bengal tiger, snow leopard, one-horned rhinoceros, red panda, and elephant. The Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation enforces wildlife laws. Buffer zone communities receive 50% of park revenue for development. Forest product harvesting requires permits from the Division Forest Office. Timber transportation requires a transportation permit.

title: Election Laws and Voting Rights in Nepal
content: Elections in Nepal are governed by the Constitution and the Election Commission Act 2073. The Election Commission conducts federal, provincial, and local elections. All citizens aged 18+ can vote. The House of Representatives has 275 members (165 first-past-the-post + 110 proportional representation). National Assembly has 59 members (56 elected by provincial assemblies + 3 nominated). Voting rights: Every citizen 18+ can register to vote at the local Election Office. Voting is done through Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) or ballot papers. Voter registration requires citizenship certificate. Vote buying and selling is punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment and NPR 50,000 fine. Election campaigning has expenditure limits per candidate. The election code of conduct prohibits using public resources for campaigning.

title: Media and Press Freedom in Nepal
content: Press freedom is guaranteed under Article 17 of the Constitution (Right to Freedom: includes press freedom). The Press Council Act 2049 established the Press Council Nepal to maintain ethical standards. Media registration is done at the Department of Information. The Working Journalist Act 2073 protects journalist rights including minimum wage, social security, and professional safety. Broadcasting is regulated by the Nepal Telecommunications Authority. The Media Council Bill proposes a self-regulatory mechanism. The Communication and Information Technology Act 2075 covers digital media. Defamation laws still apply through the Muluki Civil Code. Sedition provisions in the Criminal Code can restrict speech in limited circumstances. Journalists cannot be compelled to disclose sources except under court order for national security.

title: Women's Rights and Gender Equality in Nepal
content: The Constitution guarantees women's rights under Article 38 including the right to equal lineage (pass citizenship to children), equal property rights, access to education and health, and employment with equal pay for equal work. Women must constitute 33% of federal parliament, 50% of provincial assemblies, and 40% of local government. The Gender Equality Act 2063 prohibits gender discrimination. Sexual harassment is punishable under the Criminal Code (Section 224 - up to 3 years imprisonment). The Domestic Violence Act 2066 provides protection orders. The Trafficking and Transportation (Control) Act 2064 addresses human trafficking. Women's right to parental property is equal to sons. Maternity leave: 60 days paid. The Women Development Program provides skill training and micro-credit. She contributes to women's legal awareness.

title: Land Tenure and Tenancy Rights in Nepal
content: The Land Tenancy Act 2052 and Land Act 2021 govern landlord-tenant relationships. A registered tenancy (Mohi) gives the tenant rights to cultivate the land. Types of tenants: Adhiya (crop-sharing tenant) and Kuti (fixed-rent tenant). The landlord cannot evict a tenant without court order. Grounds for eviction: non-payment of rent for 2+ years, subletting without permission, misuse of land, and landlord's bona fide need for personal cultivation. The crop share is generally 50-50 for Adhiya tenants. Tenants have preference rights (Purvadhikar) to purchase the land if the landlord sells. Land ceiling limits: 10 Bigha (6.77 ha) in Terai, 25 Ropani (1.27 ha) in Kathmandu Valley, 70 Ropani (3.56 ha) elsewhere hills. Excess land can be confiscated and distributed to landless. The Land Reform Commission handles redistribution.

title: Local Government Operations and Services
content: Local government in Nepal operates under the Local Government Operation Act 2074. Each of the 753 local units (Metropolitan, Sub-Metropolitan, Municipality, Rural Municipality) has a Village/Municipal Assembly and a Ward Committee. Local governments handle: local infrastructure (roads, water, electricity), agriculture extension, basic health services, basic education (primary schools), local tax collection (property tax, house rent tax, entertainment tax), land use planning, local economic development, and social welfare programs. Local governments can make laws, collect revenue, and implement development projects. The Ward Office provides citizen services: birth registration, marriage registration, death registration, citizenship recommendation, and income certificate. Local tax includes property tax (up to 2.5% of assessed value) and house rent tax (10% of annual rent). Monthly ward meetings are open to citizens.

title: Banking Laws and Regulations in Nepal
content: The banking sector in Nepal is regulated by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) under the Nepal Rastra Bank Act 2058 and the Bank and Financial Institution Act (BFIA) 2073. Types of institutions: Commercial Banks (Class A), Development Banks (Class B), Finance Companies (Class C), and Microfinance Institutions (Class D). NRB sets monetary policy, regulates interest rates, and supervises banks. Key regulations: minimum capital requirement, statutory liquidity ratio (SLR), cash reserve ratio (CRR), and loan loss provisioning. Interest rates are determined by each bank's lending rate (Base Rate + premium). Deposit insurance covers up to NPR 500,000 per depositor per bank. NRB's directives limit maximum loan-to-value ratios for housing (60%) and vehicle (50%) loans. Consumer protection: banks must disclose all fees and interest clearly. Complaints can be filed at NRB's Banking and Financial Institution Regulation Department.

title: Cyber Law and Digital Rights in Nepal
content: The Electronic Transaction Act 2063 (ETA) is the primary cyber law in Nepal. It recognizes digital signatures and electronic records as legally valid. Key provisions: Unauthorized access to computer systems (up to 5 years imprisonment + NPR 200,000 fine), Hacking (up to 5 years + NPR 200,000 fine), Damage to computer system (up to 5 years + NPR 300,000 fine), Publication of illegal content (up to 5 years + NPR 200,000 fine). The Information Technology Emergency Response Team (ITERT) handles cyber incident response. The Nepal Police Cyber Bureau investigates cyber crimes. The Department of Information Technology manages IT policy. The Right to Information extends to digital records. Social media regulations require platforms to remove illegal content within 72 hours. Data protection provisions are limited under current law. The proposed Data Protection Bill will introduce comprehensive privacy protections.

title: Sexual Offenses and Rape Laws in Nepal
content: Sexual offenses in Nepal are governed by the Muluki Criminal Code 2017 (Chapter on Sexual Offenses). Rape (Section 219): A person who engages in sexual intercourse without consent commits rape. Punishment: 10-15 years imprisonment. Marital rape: recognized under Section 219 (exemption for husbands removed in 2074). Child sexual abuse: Section 220 provides for additional penalties when the victim is under 18. Attempted rape: half the maximum punishment. Statutory rape: sexual intercourse with a child under 16 is automatically considered rape. Evidence rules protect victim identity. Victim's previous sexual history is generally inadmissible. Government provides free legal aid to rape victims. The One Door Crisis Management Centers at government hospitals provide integrated services for sexual violence victims. Psychological counseling and rehabilitation services are available.

title: Electronic Transaction Act 2063 - Complete Guide
content: The Electronic Transaction Act 2063 (ETA) is Nepal's primary cyber law enacted in 2006. It provides legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures. Key offenses and penalties: (1) Unauthorized access to computer material - up to 3 years imprisonment or NPR 100,000 fine or both; (2) Unauthorized access with intent to commit offense - up to 5 years imprisonment or NPR 200,000 fine or both; (3) Damage to computer system - up to 5 years imprisonment and NPR 300,000 fine; (4) Hacking - up to 5 years imprisonment and NPR 200,000 fine; (5) Publication of illegal content - up to 5 years imprisonment and NPR 200,000 fine; (6) Breach of confidentiality and privacy - up to 3 years or NPR 100,000 or both; (7) Publishing false digital signature - up to 2 years or NPR 50,000 or both. The Act also establishes the Controller of Certifying Authorities for digital signature regulation. The Nepal Police Cyber Bureau at Narayanhiti, Kathmandu (phone 01-4779900) is the primary enforcement agency. The Information Technology Emergency Response Team (ITERT) handles cyber incident response. The Act applies to any offense committed within Nepal or affecting a computer system located in Nepal.

title: Online Scam and Digital Fraud - Victim Response Steps
content: If you are a victim of an online scam or digital fraud in Nepal, take these immediate steps: (1) Contact your bank immediately to freeze accounts and reverse unauthorized transactions. Call Nepal Rastra Bank helpline at 01-4511155. (2) File a complaint at the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau within 24 hours. Visit their office at Narayanhiti, Kathmandu or call 01-4779900. You can also file online at cyberbureau.nepalpolice.gov.np. (3) Preserve ALL evidence: screenshots of conversations, transaction receipts, emails, WhatsApp/Facebook messages, bank statements, website URLs, and phone numbers. (4) For social media scams (fake Facebook profiles, Marketplace fraud), also report to the platform itself. (5) For investment scams (ponzi schemes, crypto fraud), file a complaint with the Securities Board of Nepal (SEBON) and Nepal Rastra Bank. (6) File a written complaint (FIR) at your nearest District Police Office. The police must register your complaint under Section 155 of the Criminal Procedure Code. If they refuse, approach the Superintendent of Police. (7) The Cyber Bureau investigates under the Electronic Transaction Act 2063. Offenders face up to 5 years imprisonment and fines up to NPR 200,000 for hacking and NPR 300,000 for computer damage. (8) Contact a cyber law lawyer for legal representation. Recovery of lost funds is possible through court order. Prevention tips: never share OTP or banking PIN, verify website URLs before payment, use secure payment gateways, and be cautious of too-good-to-be-true offers.

title: Social Media Laws and Cyber Bullying
content: Social media use in Nepal is regulated under the Electronic Transaction Act 2063 and the Criminal Code 2017. Cyber bullying includes posting offensive comments, sharing private photos without consent, creating fake profiles to harass, and online stalking. Penalties: (1) Publishing illegal content on social media (Section 47 of ETA) - up to 5 years imprisonment and/or NPR 200,000 fine. (2) Harassment through electronic means - treated as criminal harassment under the Criminal Code. Victims should: (1) Save all evidence (screenshots, URLs, dates). (2) Block the harasser and report to the social media platform. (3) File a complaint at the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau (01-4779900). (4) For urgent cases involving threats, file an FIR at your local police station. (5) Seek a court protection order if harassment continues. Impersonation (fake accounts using your identity) is a specific offense under the ETA. Defamation on social media can be pursued both as a criminal case (up to 1 year imprisonment) and civil case (damages). The Right to Privacy is protected under Article 28 of the Constitution of Nepal 2015.

title: Human Trafficking and Transportation (Control) Act 2064
content: The Human Trafficking and Transportation (Control) Act 2064 (2007) is Nepal's primary law against human trafficking and smuggling. Key provisions: Trafficking is defined as selling or buying a person for any purpose, forced prostitution, organ removal, or forced labor (Section 4). Transportation is defined as moving a person across borders for exploitation (Section 5). Penalties: Trafficking - 10-20 years imprisonment and fine up to NPR 500,000; Transportation - 5-15 years imprisonment and fine up to NPR 300,000; Attempt - half the maximum punishment. Aggravated offenses: trafficking of minors attracts life imprisonment. The National Human Rights Commission monitors anti-trafficking efforts. District committees coordinate prevention and rescue. Victims are entitled to rehabilitation, compensation, and protection. Identity of victims is protected. Foreign nationals involved in trafficking face the same penalties plus deportation. The Act also covers cyber trafficking and online exploitation.

title: Money Laundering Prevention Act 2064
content: The Money Laundering Prevention Act 2064 (2007) criminalizes money laundering in Nepal. It is enforced by the Nepal Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) under Nepal Rastra Bank. Money laundering is defined as concealing or disguising the proceeds of crime (Section 3). Predicate offenses include drug trafficking, human trafficking, corruption, fraud, terrorism, and tax evasion. Penalties: 1-6 months imprisonment or fine equal to twice the value of laundered property or both. Entities must report suspicious transactions above NPR 1 million. Banks, financial institutions, remittance companies, and casinos are obligated to implement Know Your Customer (KYC) and Customer Due Diligence (CDD). Failure to report suspicious transactions carries penalties. The Act allows freezing and confiscation of property derived from criminal activity. International cooperation in money laundering investigations is provided under mutual legal assistance provisions.

title: Evidence Act 2031 - Rules of Evidence in Nepal
content: The Evidence Act 2031 (1974) governs the admissibility of evidence in Nepali courts. Key principles: Burden of proof lies with the person who asserts a fact (Section 3). Relevant facts are admissible unless excluded by law (Section 4). Confessions made under duress, threat, or promise are not admissible (Section 9). Confession to a police officer is not admissible. Dying declarations (statements made by a person about to die) are admissible as evidence (Section 13). Documentary evidence includes primary evidence (original document) and secondary evidence (certified copies). Electronic evidence is admissible under the Electronic Transaction Act 2063. Witness testimony must be given under oath (Section 17). Character evidence is generally not admissible in civil cases but may be relevant in criminal cases (Section 22). Presumptions: a person is presumed innocent until proven guilty; possession of stolen goods after theft raises a presumption of guilt. Expert opinion is admissible on foreign law, science, handwriting, and fingerprint analysis.

title: Arms and Ammunition Act 2019 - Weapons Law
content: The Arms and Ammunition Act 2019 (1962) regulates the possession, use, and sale of weapons in Nepal. License required for all firearms. Categories: Category A (prohibited - automatic weapons, explosives, bombs) for military/security forces only; Category B (restricted - handguns, rifles, shotguns) requires license; Category C (less lethal - air guns, pellet guns) requires permit. License application at District Administration Office: minimum age 21, criminal background check, valid reason (self-defense, sports, profession). License valid for 5 years and renewable. Penalties for unlicensed possession: up to 7 years imprisonment for Category A, up to 5 years for Category B, fine and confiscation for Category C. Carrying firearms in public places without permit is prohibited. Import/export requires Home Ministry approval. Ammunition limit: up to 100 rounds per licensed weapon. Sharp weapons (khukuri, swords) over certain sizes require registration.

title: Prison Act 2019 - Prisoners Rights and Prison Administration
content: The Prison Act 2019 (1962) governs prison administration in Nepal. Types of prisoners: convicts (sentenced), undertrials (awaiting trial), and civil prisoners (debt). Prisoners must be classified by age, gender, and offense type. Male and female prisoners must be kept separate. Juvenile prisoners are kept in separate correctional facilities. Minimum standards: adequate food, clothing, bedding, medical care, and sanitation. Prisoners have the right to communicate with family through letters and visits (frequency determined by prison rules). Undertrials are entitled to bail under the Criminal Procedure Code. The Prison Rules prescribe work and vocational training for rehabilitation. Prisoners can submit complaints to the Prison Management Committee, the District Judge, and the National Human Rights Commission. Early release may be granted for good conduct after serving two-thirds of sentence. The death sentence is not imposed on minors, pregnant women, or persons with mental illness. Capital punishment can be commuted by the President.

title: Arbitration Act 2055 - Arbitration in Nepal
content: The Arbitration Act 2055 (1999) governs domestic and international commercial arbitration in Nepal. Arbitration is a private dispute resolution method where parties agree to submit disputes to an arbitral tribunal instead of court. The Arbitration Act is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law. Key features: Arbitration agreement must be in writing (Section 4). Arbitral tribunal consists of 1 or 3 arbitrators. Parties can agree on the procedure. The tribunal can grant interim measures (Section 11). Arbitral award must be in writing, signed, and state reasons (Section 22). Domestic awards can be challenged in the High Court within 35 days on limited grounds (Section 27). International awards are subject to enforcement under the New York Convention. Nepal is a signatory to the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. The Nepal Council of Arbitration (NeCA) promotes arbitration. Court intervention is limited to specific grounds including incapacity of parties, invalid arbitration agreement, or violation of natural justice. Arbitration is faster (3-6 months) than court litigation.

title: Insolvency Act 2063 - Bankruptcy and Restructuring
content: The Insolvency Act 2063 (2006) governs bankruptcy and insolvency proceedings for businesses and individuals in Nepal. Types of proceedings: (1) Corporate insolvency - for companies unable to pay debts; (2) Personal insolvency - for individuals; (3) Cross-border insolvency. A debtor or creditor can file a petition at the Debt Recovery Tribunal or the High Court. The court appoints a liquidator or administrator to manage assets. Insolvency triggers: inability to pay debts as they fall due, liabilities exceeding assets. The moratorium (automatic stay) stops all legal actions against the debtor. Voluntary restructuring is possible through a scheme of arrangement approved by 75% of creditors (by value). Preferential payments: secured creditors are paid first, followed by employees (up to 3 months wages), government taxes, and unsecured creditors. Fraudulent transfers before insolvency can be reversed. Individual insolvency: debtor can apply for discharge after 5 years. Bankruptcy carries reputational consequences and restrictions on holding directorships. The Insolvency Act aims to balance debtor rehabilitation with creditor protection.

title: Limitation Act 2049 - Time Limits for Filing Cases
content: The Limitation Act 2049 (1992) prescribes time limits (statutes of limitation) for filing different types of cases in Nepal. Basic rules: Limitation runs from the date the cause of action arises.
