Key limitation periods: Civil suits (general) - 3 years; Breach of contract - 1 year; Recovery of movable property - 6 months; Recovery of immovable property - 12 years; Adverse possession of immovable property - 12 years; Partition of property - 3 years from demand; Debt recovery - 2 years from due date; Gift of immovable property - 1 year; Succession/inheritance - 3 years from death; Defamation - 6 months; Writ petitions - 35 days from cause of action; Criminal appeals to High Court - 70 days from judgment; Civil appeals to High Court - 90 days from judgment; Supreme Court appeals - 21 days. Limitation is extended if the plaintiff is a minor, insane, or prevented by force majeure. The court can condone delay in certain circumstances. Filing after limitation renders the case time-barred and the claim unenforceable.

title: Senior Citizens Act 2063 - Rights of Elderly
content: The Senior Citizens Act 2063 (2006) protects the rights of persons aged 60 and above in Nepal. Key provisions: Senior citizens have the right to respect, maintenance, and protection from family members (Section 3). Children must provide food, clothing, shelter, and medical care for elderly parents. Abandonment or neglect of senior citizens is punishable with up to 3 months imprisonment or NPR 10,000 fine or both (Section 18). The government provides a monthly social security allowance of NPR 4,000 to all senior citizens (age 70+ general, 60+ for Dalits and Karnali residents). Free medical treatment at government hospitals. Senior citizens get 50% discount on public transport (Section 5). Priority queues at all public offices. Legal aid is available free of charge for senior citizens. The old-age home (Vriddhashram) is provided by the government for destitute elderly. Senior Citizens' Funds support welfare programs. Abuse or exploitation of senior citizens is a criminal offense under the Criminal Code. Property rights of senior citizens are protected - children cannot take property by force. The Senior Citizens Rehabilitation Center provides residential care for abandoned elderly.

title: Caste Discrimination and Untouchability Laws - Dalit Rights
content: Caste-based discrimination and untouchability are prohibited under the Constitution of Nepal 2015 (Articles 18 and 24). The Caste-based Discrimination and Untouchability (Offense and Punishment) Act 2068 (2011) provides the legal framework. The Act prohibits: practicing untouchability in any form (Section 3), restricting access to public places, temples, hotels, schools, hospitals, or water sources based on caste (Section 4), and preventing inter-caste marriage (Section 5). Penalties: up to 3 years imprisonment and/or fine up to NPR 50,000 for individuals (Section 8). Higher penalties for public officials who commit or condone discrimination. Collective punishment for groups committing caste violence. The National Dalit Commission monitors implementation. Victims can file complaints at the District Police Office or the National Human Rights Commission. The State must provide free legal aid to victims. Hate speech based on caste is punishable. Inter-caste marriage is incentivized with NPR 100,000 government allowance. Education scholarships are reserved for Dalit students. The government has reservation quotas for Dalits in public employment, education, and political representation.

title: Persons with Disabilities Rights Act 2074
content: The Persons with Disabilities Rights Act 2074 (2017) protects and promotes the rights of persons with disabilities in Nepal. PWD includes physical, sensory (deaf, blind), intellectual, mental, and multiple disabilities. Key rights: Right to accessibility in public buildings, transportation, and information; Right to education in inclusive settings; Right to health services; Right to employment without discrimination; Right to social security allowance (NPR 3,000 per month). The Act prohibits discrimination against PWDs in employment, education, and access to services (Section 13). Employers must make reasonable accommodations. The government must ensure accessible public infrastructure. Sign language interpretation must be provided in public offices for the deaf. Disability ID card (Apangata Parichaya Patra) issued by local government provides access to benefits. The National Federation of the Disabled Nepal (NFDN) advocates for disability rights. Penalties for discrimination against PWD: up to 1 year imprisonment or NPR 30,000 fine or both. Quota: 5% reservation in public service employment for PWDs. Building codes require accessibility features in new construction.

title: Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act 2075 (FITTA)
content: The Foreign Investment and Technology Transfer Act 2075 (2018) (FITTA) governs foreign investment in Nepal. The Department of Industry (DoI) approves foreign investments. Minimum foreign investment threshold: NPR 50 million (approx USD 400,000). Permitted sectors: most manufacturing, services, energy, infrastructure, tourism, and IT. Prohibited sectors: cottage industries, arms and ammunition, explosives, tobacco/alcohol, real estate (except construction), and personal services (hairdressing, tailoring). Foreign investors can own 100% equity in most sectors. Some sectors have minimum Nepali ownership requirements (e.g., travel agencies, consultancy services). Repatriation: foreign investors can repatriate profits, dividends, and capital after tax payment. Technology transfer agreements require DoI approval. Dispute resolution: disputes can be settled through arbitration as per the Arbitration Act 2055 or international arbitration. Tax incentives: income tax holiday for certain industries (5-10 years), customs duty exemptions on capital goods. Intellectual property protection under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act 2022. Investment protection: foreign investments cannot be expropriated without compensation.

title: Industrial Enterprises Act 2020 - Industry Registration and Incentives
content: The Industrial Enterprises Act 2020 governs industries in Nepal. Industry classifications: Micro Industry (investment up to NPR 20 million), Small Industry (NPR 20 million - 100 million), Medium Industry (NPR 100 million - 500 million), and Large Industry (above NPR 500 million). Registration: Cottage and Small Industries at the Department of Cottage and Small Industries; Medium and Large industries at the Department of Industry. Special categories: export-oriented, import-substituting, tourism, agriculture, energy, IT, and mineral industries receive additional incentives. Incentives include: income tax exemption for 5-20 years depending on industry type and location (remote/undeveloped areas get longer exemptions); customs duty exemptions on machinery and equipment; concessionary loan facilities. Industries in Special Economic Zones (SEZ) get additional benefits. One Window Service at the Investment Board Nepal for large investments. Environmental Impact Assessment is required for large industries. Factories must comply with labor, safety, and environmental standards. Annual industry census data must be submitted to the Department of Industry.

title: Cooperative Act 2048 - Cooperative Societies
content: The Cooperative Act 2048 (1992) governs cooperative societies in Nepal. A cooperative is a voluntary organization of persons with common economic interests. Types: Savings and Credit Cooperatives, Agricultural Cooperatives, Multipurpose Cooperatives, Consumer Cooperatives, and Producer Cooperatives. Registration at the Department of Cooperatives (central) or District Cooperative Office. Minimum 7 members required for registration. Governance: General Assembly (supreme body), Board of Directors (elected), and Audit Committee. Cooperative Principles: voluntary membership, democratic control (one member one vote), member economic participation, autonomy, education, cooperation among cooperatives, and concern for community. Savings and Credit Cooperatives must register with Nepal Rastra Bank for deposit-taking activities. Audit is mandatory every year. Members must be refunded their share capital on exit. Net profits are distributed among members as dividends (maximum 15%) and allocated to reserves (minimum 25%). The Cooperative Supervision Division regulates compliance. Penalties for misuse of cooperative funds include 1-5 years imprisonment. The Nepal Cooperative Federation promotes cooperative development.

title: Securities Act 2063 - Stock Market and Capital Markets
content: The Securities Act 2063 (2006) regulates securities markets in Nepal. The Securities Board of Nepal (SEBON) is the capital market regulator. Key provisions: Securities include shares, debentures, bonds, mutual funds, and derivatives. Any company issuing securities to the public must register a prospectus with SEBON (Section 10). Insider trading is prohibited (Section 47). Market manipulation and false trading are criminal offenses (Section 48). Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) is the only stock exchange. Listed companies must: disclose financial results quarterly, maintain proper books, provide annual reports. Rights of shareholders: attend AGM, vote, receive dividends, inspect financial records. Broker regulation: stock brokers must be licensed. Central Depository System (CDS) handles dematerialized (demat) shares. Minimum public offering: 10% of issued capital for public companies. Penalties: insider trading - up to 5 years imprisonment and NPR 500,000 fine; market manipulation - up to 5 years and NPR 300,000 fine; unlicensed trading - up to 3 years and fine. Capital gains tax: 5% for shares held less than 1 year, 7.5% for longer. IPOs are regulated by SEBON guidelines.

title: Public Procurement Act 2063 - Government Contracts and Tendering
content: The Public Procurement Act 2063 (2006) governs procurement by public entities in Nepal. The Public Procurement Monitoring Office (PPMO) sets policies. Procurement methods: (1) Sealed Quotation - up to NPR 200,000; (2) Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS) for services; (3) International Competitive Bidding (ICB) for large foreign-funded projects; (4) Direct Procurement in exceptional circumstances (Section 23). Procurement thresholds: Public entities must form a Procurement Review Committee for contracts above NPR 5 million. Bidding documents must be publicly available. Evaluation criteria: lowest evaluated responsive bid. Bid security (typically 2-3% of estimated cost) is required. Performance guarantee (5% of contract value) must be submitted. Preference: Nepali suppliers get 10% price preference in evaluation. Timeframes: minimum 30 days for international bidding. Dispute resolution: Review Committee, then Public Procurement Appellate Court within 35 days. Blacklisting: contractors who breach contracts can be blacklisted for up to 3 years. Transparency: all procurement decisions must be published in the PPMO portal.

title: Advocates Act 2055 - Legal Profession and Lawyers Regulation
content: The Advocates Act 2055 (1999) regulates the legal profession in Nepal. Nepal Bar Council issues licenses to practice law. Requirements: Bachelor of Laws (LLB) degree from a recognized university, 6 months internship at a senior advocate's office, and pass the Bar Council exam. Types of advocates: Senior Advocate (20+ years experience, designated by Nepal Bar Council), Advocate (licensed practitioner), and Government Attorney (public prosecutor). Advocates must register with the Bar Council and obtain a practicing certificate renewed annually. Code of conduct: advocates must maintain client confidentiality, avoid conflict of interest, not appear against a former client on the same matter, and not advertise undignifiedly. Fee disputes are settled by the Nepal Bar Association Fee Committee. Disciplinary action: Bar Council can suspend or cancel licenses for professional misconduct (up to 3 years suspension). Advocates cannot guarantee success in a case. Foreign lawyers cannot appear in Nepali courts without permission. The Bar Association provides pro bono legal aid. Advocates have immunity for statements made in court.

title: Notary Public Act 2063 - Notary Services
content: The Notary Public Act 2063 (2006) governs notary public services in Nepal. A notary public is a legal professional authorized to certify documents, administer oaths, and authenticate signatures. Appointment: the Minister of Law appoints notaries on recommendation of the Ministry of Law and Justice. Qualifications: Nepali citizen, advocate with at least 5 years practice, no criminal record, and completion of notary training. Powers: (1) Certify copies of documents as true copies; (2) Certify signatures; (3) Administer oaths and affirmations; (4) Attest affidavits; (5) Verify translations; (6) Record protests of negotiable instruments. Documents notarized: property transfer deeds, power of attorney, affidavits, agreements, and declarations. Notarized documents are considered public documents and have evidentiary value. A notary cannot notarize their own document or documents where they are personally interested. Notary fee is regulated (typically NPR 100-500 per document). Notaries must maintain a register of their official acts. Misconduct: can be penalized by suspension or removal. Foreign documents require notarization and then apostille or consular legalization for use abroad.

title: Water Resources Act 2049 - Water Rights and Hydropower
content: The Water Resources Act 2049 (1992) governs the use of water resources in Nepal. Water is a state-owned resource. The Act covers: drinking water, irrigation, hydropower, industrial use, and navigation. Water use requires a license from the Department of Water Resources (Section 6). Categories of licenses: Survey License (to study feasibility), Generation License (for hydropower), and Distribution License. Domestic use and small-scale irrigation do not require licenses. Water rights hierarchy: drinking water has highest priority, then irrigation, then hydropower, then industrial use. The Water Resources Strategy provides long-term planning. Hydropower Development Policy 2058 promotes private sector investment in hydropower. Royalty rates: hydropower projects pay royalty based on generation capacity. Environmental Impact Assessment is required for large water projects. Water disputes are resolved by the Water Resources Tribunal. Pollution of water sources is punishable. The Act protects riparian rights of downstream users. Water Users' Associations manage local irrigation systems. The Water Resources Regulation 2050 provides detailed procedures for licensing and supervision.

title: Telecommunications Act 2053 - Telecom and Internet Regulation
content: The Telecommunications Act 2053 (1996) regulates telecommunications and internet services in Nepal. The Nepal Telecommunications Authority (NTA) is the regulatory body. Nepal Doorsanchar Company Limited (NDCL/Telecom) is the state-owned telecom provider. Key provisions: Telecom service requires a license from NTA (Section 5). License types: Basic Telecom Service, Cellular Mobile Service, Internet Service Provider (ISP), VSAT, and Infrastructure Provider. Telecom companies must provide interconnection to other licensed operators. Spectrum allocation is managed by NTA. Universal Service Fund supports telecom access in remote areas. Quality of Service standards are prescribed by NTA. Consumer protection: service providers must disclose tariffs, provide itemized bills, and handle complaints. Penalties for illegal telecom equipment: confiscation and fine. Cyber cafes must maintain user logs. Interception of communications requires court order for national security (Section 41). Radio and television broadcasting licenses are also regulated by NTA. The Telecommunications (Amendment) Act 2073 introduced provisions for internet governance and OTT services. Penalty for unauthorized spectrum use: up to 5 years imprisonment and NPR 500,000 fine.

title: Social Welfare Act 2049 - Social Protection Programs
content: The Social Welfare Act 2049 (1992) governs social welfare programs in Nepal. The Social Welfare Council coordinates and monitors social welfare activities. Types of social security: (1) Old Age Allowance - NPR 4,000/month for 70+ (60+ for Dalits and Karnali residents); (2) Single Woman Allowance - NPR 3,000/month (widows, divorced, unmarried 40+); (3) Disability Allowance - NPR 3,000/month for fully disabled, NPR 1,500/month for partially disabled; (4) Child Grant - NPR 500/month per child (up to 2 children) for families in Karnali and remote areas; (5) Endangered Ethnic Group Allowance. The Senior Citizens Act 2063, Child Grant, and other social security programs operate under this framework. NGOs and INGOs working in social welfare must register with the Social Welfare Council. Foreign funding for social projects requires SWC approval. The Act governs orphanages, elderly homes, and rehabilitation centers. The Women Development Program provides skill training and micro-credit to women. The Prime Minister's Education Scholarship supports poor students. The Act requires annual reporting by registered organizations. The SWC can investigate and suspend organizations violating regulations.

title: Food Act 2033 and Food Safety Regulations
content: The Food Act 2033 (1976) ensures food safety and quality in Nepal. The Department of Food Technology and Quality Control (DFTQC) regulates food standards. Key provisions: Adulteration of food is prohibited (Section 4). Selling substandard, misbranded, or expired food is punishable. Imported food must meet Nepali food standards. Food businesses must register with DFTQC. Food inspectors can take samples for testing. Laboratories are authorized to test food quality. Penalties for food adulteration: up to 5 years imprisonment and/or fine up to NPR 200,000 (Section 14). Manufacturing unhygienic food: fine up to NPR 50,000. Selling expired products: fine up to NPR 25,000. Repeat offenses attract double penalties. The Food Regulation 2027 specifies labeling requirements: product name, ingredients, net weight, manufacturing date, expiry date, manufacturer details, and price. The DFTQC has the power to confiscate and destroy unsafe food. Hotels and restaurants must maintain hygiene standards. Consumers can file complaints at the DFTQC or the Department of Commerce. The Food Act also covers food additives, preservatives, and pesticide residue limits. The Act applies to all food businesses including street vendors and restaurants.

title: Extradition Act 2071 - International Criminal Cooperation
content: The Extradition Act 2071 (2014) governs the extradition of fugitives to and from Nepal. Extradition is the process by which a person accused or convicted of a crime is surrendered by one country to another. Nepal can extradite persons only where a bilateral extradition treaty exists (Section 3). Extradition is not granted for political offenses, military offenses, or where the person may face torture or death penalty (Section 9). Requirements: the offense must be punishable by at least 1 year imprisonment in both countries (dual criminality). The process: request through diplomatic channels; government reviews; District Court hearing; government decision (Section 11-16). Nepal has extradition treaties with India, China, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and several other countries. Provisional arrest pending extradition request is possible in urgent cases. Nepal also provides mutual legal assistance in criminal matters under the Mutual Legal Assistance Act 2070. The government can refuse extradition if it is for prosecution based on race, religion, nationality, or political opinion. Transit of extradited persons through Nepal requires permission. The Act is administered by the Ministry of Law in coordination with the Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

title: Nepal Rastra Bank Act 2058 - Central Banking and Monetary Policy
content: The Nepal Rastra Bank Act 2058 (2001) establishes and governs Nepal's central bank. Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) is the sole monetary authority with powers to: issue currency (Nepali rupee), formulate and implement monetary policy, regulate the banking and financial sector, manage foreign exchange reserves, act as banker to the government, and supervise payment systems. The Governor heads NRB, appointed by the President on government recommendation (Section 18). Monetary policy tools: Bank Rate (currently 7.5%), Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR), Open Market Operations, and Repo/Reverse Repo. NRB sets the Base Rate for commercial banks. NRB regulates interest rates through policy rates and directives. Foreign exchange policy: pegged to Indian rupee at NPR 160 = INR 100. NRB issues licenses for banks, financial institutions, microfinance, and remittance companies. NRB conducts on-site and off-site supervision of financial institutions. It can impose penalties, restrict activities, or liquidate non-compliant institutions. NRB manages the Deposit and Credit Guarantee Corporation (deposit insurance up to NPR 500,000). Annual inflation target and money supply targets are announced in the monetary policy.

title: Cryptocurrency and Digital Currency Ban in Nepal
content: Cryptocurrency is completely illegal in Nepal. The Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) first declared Bitcoin trading illegal in August 2017 and has reaffirmed the ban through multiple notices (2021, 2023, 2024). The statutory basis spans three Acts: Foreign Exchange (Regulation) Act 2019 (Section 9(c) and 17), Nepal Rastra Bank Act 2058 (Sections 52, 61, 95), and the Act Restricting Investment Abroad 2021 (Section 3). Prohibited activities include: trading, mining, investing, holding, brokering, accepting as payment, promoting/advertising, and using VPN to access foreign crypto exchanges. All cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, BNB, Solana, XRP, all altcoins, NFTs, and stablecoins) are banned. Penalties: fine of 1x to 3x the transaction value plus imprisonment up to 3 years under the Foreign Exchange Act (up to 7 years under NRB Act Section 95 for high-value cases), plus full asset confiscation. Enforcement by the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB) Cyber Bureau and Nepal Police. Cases are tried in District Court. Nepal is developing a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) but private crypto remains banned. Digital wallets (eSewa, Khalti, IME Pay) are legal and regulated by NRB with daily limits of NPR 50,000-100,000.

title: Online Gambling, Betting and Gaming Laws
content: Online gambling and betting are illegal in Nepal under the Gambling Act 2020 (1963) and the Electronic Transaction Act 2063. The Gambling Act prohibits operating or participating in any gambling house, online betting platform, or lottery scheme. Online cricket betting, casino games, poker, and sports betting are prohibited. Nepal also strictly prohibits accessing foreign gambling websites. Using VPN to bypass the ban is also illegal. Penalties: operating gambling - up to 3 years imprisonment and fine up to NPR 50,000; participating - up to 1 year imprisonment or fine up to NPR 5,000 or both. The Cyber Bureau investigates online gambling operations. Social media-based gambling and betting groups are also targeted. Fantasy sports platforms may be considered gambling if involving money. Lotteries are only legal when operated by the government (Nepal Lottery). Casinos are only legal in licensed 5-star hotels for foreign tourists - Nepali citizens are prohibited from entering or gambling in Nepali casinos. Online rummy, card games for money, and esports betting fall under gambling prohibitions. Internet Service Providers must block gambling websites on NRB and NTA directives.

title: Digital Piracy and Copyright Infringement Online
content: Digital piracy in Nepal is addressed under the Copyright Act 2058 (2002) and the Electronic Transaction Act 2063. Copyright infringement includes unauthorized downloading, sharing, or distribution of copyrighted content (movies, music, software, books, games) through torrents, streaming sites, or social media. Penalties: Copyright infringement - up to 3 years imprisonment or fine up to NPR 100,000 or both. Repeat infringement doubles the penalty. The Copyright Registrar Office handles complaints. ISPs can be ordered to block infringing websites. Software piracy: using unlicensed software is a civil and criminal offense. The Business Software Alliance (BSA) monitors software piracy in Nepal. Movie piracy: unauthorized recording or distribution of films in theaters is punishable. Book piracy: unauthorized printing or digital distribution of books is illegal. Fair use exceptions exist for education, research, and personal use. Open-source software and Creative Commons licensing are recognized. For trademark infringement online (counterfeit goods, fake websites), complaints can be filed at the Department of Industry and Nepal Police. Patent infringement online also falls under the Patent, Design and Trademark Act 2022. The Nepal Copyright Act also protects neighboring rights (performers, broadcasters, producers).

title: Cyber Crime Against Children and Child Online Protection
content: Cyber crimes against children in Nepal are governed by the Children's Act 2075 (2018), Electronic Transaction Act 2063, and the Muluki Criminal Code 2017. Key offenses: (1) Child pornography - production, distribution, or possession of sexual images of minors is punishable under Section 220 of the Criminal Code with 10-15 years imprisonment (higher than adult pornography penalties). (2) Online grooming - adults contacting children online for sexual purposes is a criminal offense. (3) Cyber bullying of minors - targeting children through social media harassment, threats, or humiliation. (4) Identity theft of minors - using a child's identity for fraud. (5) Sextortion - threatening to share intimate images of minors. (6) Live streaming of child sexual abuse - treated as aggravated human trafficking. (7) Luring children through online gaming platforms or social media. Reporting: complaints to the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau (01-4779900) or the National Child Helpline 104. The Central Child Welfare Board coordinates child protection. Schools must implement internet safety programs. Parents are advised to monitor children's online activities. Internet cafes must not allow minors to access adult content. The ITERT (Information Technology Emergency Response Team) handles takedown of child sexual abuse material hosted in Nepal.

title: Data Protection, Privacy Laws and Upcoming Legislation
content: Data protection in Nepal is currently governed by multiple laws rather than a single comprehensive data protection act. Key legal provisions: (1) Right to Privacy - Article 28 of the Constitution of Nepal 2015 guarantees the right to privacy. (2) Electronic Transaction Act 2063 - Section 54 on breach of confidentiality and privacy with penalties up to 3 years imprisonment and NPR 100,000 fine. (3) Telecommunications Act 2053 - prohibits unauthorized interception of communications. (4) Labor Act 2074 - employee data protection. The proposed Data Protection Bill (currently under drafting by the Ministry of Communications and IT) will introduce: mandatory data breach notification, consent requirements for data collection, data localization requirements, appointment of Data Protection Officer for large entities, rights of data subjects (access, correction, deletion, portability), cross-border data transfer restrictions, penalties up to 2% of annual turnover for violations, and establishment of a Data Protection Authority. Currently, organizations handling personal data must implement reasonable security practices under Section 54 of ETA. The right to information (RTI) under the Right to Information Act 2064 balances privacy with transparency. Biometric data collection by government requires consent. The Privacy (Protection) Bill is also under consideration. Enforcement agencies include Cyber Bureau and NTA for data breach incidents.

title: Ransomware, Malware, Phishing and Hacking Laws
content: Cyber attacks including ransomware, malware, phishing, and unauthorized access are criminal offenses under the Electronic Transaction Act 2063 and the Muluki Criminal Code 2017. Key offenses and penalties: (1) Ransomware - deploying malicious software that encrypts data and demands payment. Treated as computer damage under ETA Section 45: up to 5 years imprisonment and NPR 300,000 fine. (2) Malware distribution - creating or spreading viruses, trojans, worms, spyware. Penalty: up to 5 years imprisonment and/or NPR 200,000 fine. (3) Phishing - creating fake websites or emails to steal credentials. Treated as unauthorized access and fraud: up to 5 years imprisonment and NPR 200,000 fine. (4) DDoS attacks - disrupting online services - up to 5 years imprisonment and NPR 300,000 fine. (5) Hacking into systems (Section 44 ETA) - unauthorized access to computer material: up to 3 years or NPR 100,000 or both; unauthorized access with criminal intent: up to 5 years or NPR 200,000 or both. (6) Identity theft for cyber crimes - additional penalties. Victims should: disconnect infected devices, preserve evidence, file complaint at Cyber Bureau (01-4779900), contact ITERT for incident response, and notify affected parties. Organizations must implement cybersecurity measures. Banks and financial institutions must follow NRB's Cybersecurity Framework. The National Cyber Security Policy 2073 guides national cybersecurity. Reporting cyber attacks promptly increases chances of investigation and recovery.

title: Cyber Stalking, Online Harassment and Revenge Porn
content: Cyber stalking and online harassment in Nepal are addressed under the Electronic Transaction Act 2063 and the Muluki Criminal Code 2017. Key offenses: (1) Cyber stalking - repeatedly following, monitoring, or contacting someone online causing fear or distress. Punishable under Criminal Code Section 224 (harassment) up to 3 years imprisonment. (2) Revenge porn - sharing intimate images without consent. Under ETA Section 47 (publishing illegal content): up to 5 years imprisonment and/or NPR 200,000 fine. (3) Online threats - sending threatening messages via social media, email, or messaging apps. (4) Doxing - publishing someone's private contact information online with malicious intent. (5) Impersonation / fake profiles - creating fake accounts to harass. (6) Trolling and hate speech - targeted abuse based on gender, caste, religion, or sexual orientation. (7) Sextortion - threatening to share intimate content unless demands are met. Victims should: (1) Do not engage with the harasser. (2) Save all evidence (screenshots, messages, emails, URLs, metadata). (3) Block the harasser on all platforms. (4) Report to the social media platform. (5) File a complaint at the Cyber Bureau (01-4779900). (6) Seek a protection order from the court. (7) For revenge porn, victims can request immediate takedown under ITERT emergency procedures. The law protects victim identity during proceedings. Cyber stalking is increasingly prosecuted under both criminal and cyber laws.

title: Deepfakes, AI-Generated Content and Synthetic Media Law
content: Deepfakes and AI-generated content in Nepal are regulated under the Electronic Transaction Act 2063, the Muluki Criminal Code 2017, the Copyright Act 2058, and the Right to Privacy (Article 28 of Constitution). Key legal issues: (1) Deepfake pornography - creating sexually explicit synthetic content using someone's likeness without consent. This constitutes revenge porn under ETA Section 47, defamation under Criminal Code Section 269, and violation of privacy. Penalties: up to 5 years imprisonment and/or NPR 200,000 fine. (2) Deepfake fraud - using AI-generated audio/video to impersonate individuals for financial scams (e.g., fake CEO voice calls). Treated as fraud and identity theft. (3) AI-generated disinformation - creating fake news videos or audio of public figures. Falls under defamation and electronic fraud. (4) Synthetic media for political manipulation - using AI to create false campaign materials. (5) AI impersonation of deceased persons for exploitation. (6) Authorized uses: AI-generated content for entertainment, satire (with clear labeling), education, and art may be protected under free speech (Article 17) if it does not harm reputation or privacy. The Cyber Bureau has a dedicated unit for deepfake investigations. Proposed AI governance framework is being drafted by the Ministry of Communications. Victims of harmful deepfakes should: (1) Document the content (URLs, timestamps). (2) Request platform takedown. (3) File complaint at Cyber Bureau. (4) Contact ITERT for emergency removal. (5) Pursue defamation or privacy case in court. Social media platforms are required to remove harmful synthetic content within 72 hours of notice under ETA.

title: Digital Wallets, Payment Systems and E-Banking Regulation
content: Digital payment systems in Nepal are regulated by Nepal Rastra Bank under the Payment and Settlement System Directive. Licensed Payment Service Providers (PSPs) include eSewa, Khalti, IME Pay, PrabhuPay, and others. Payment System Operators (PSOs) include connectivity providers. Key regulations: (1) PSPs must obtain NRB license with minimum paid-up capital requirements, secure IT infrastructure, cybersecurity compliance, and KYC/AML systems. (2) Transaction limits: KYC-verified users - daily limit NPR 50,000-100,000, monthly limit NPR 5-10 lakhs, wallet balance limit NPR 50,000. (3) QR payments limit: daily NPR 100,000, monthly NPR 1,000,000. (4) Fund transfers between wallets: daily NPR 25,000-50,000. (5) Bank transfers via wallet: daily NPR 100,000 limit. (6) Digital wallets must maintain separate escrow accounts for user funds. (7) Mobile banking is regulated under NRB's Electronic Banking Guidelines. (8) Internet banking requires two-factor authentication. (9) Liability for unauthorized transactions: banks must reimburse if reported within 3 days (up to 7 days for negligence). (10) Card fraud (ATM, credit, debit): governed by Banking Offenses Act 2064 with penalties up to 10 years imprisonment. (11) QR code fraud and payment gateway fraud are addressed under ETA. Digital payment fraud victims should immediately report to their bank, NRB helpline (01-4511155), and the Cyber Bureau. NRB's Payment Systems Department supervises compliance.

title: E-Commerce Law, Online Marketplace and Digital Consumer Protection
content: E-commerce in Nepal is governed by the Electronic Transaction Act 2063, Consumer Protection Act 2075, and the Directives on Electronic Commerce issued by the Department of Commerce. Key provisions: (1) E-commerce platforms must register as a business and obtain PAN/VAT. (2) Online sellers must provide accurate product descriptions, clear pricing including all charges, delivery timelines, and return/refund policies. (3) Consumers have the right to cancel online orders within 48 hours for any reason (cooling-off period). (4) Refunds must be processed within 15 days of cancellation or return. (5) E-commerce platforms are liable for counterfeit or defective products sold through their marketplace if they do not verify sellers. (6) Cross-border e-commerce is subject to customs duties and Nepal Rastra Bank foreign exchange regulations (limit NPR 50,000 per transaction for online imports). (7) Social media commerce (Facebook Marketplace, Instagram shops, TikTok shops) is regulated like any e-commerce activity. (8) Misleading or false advertising online is prohibited. (9) Data privacy: e-commerce platforms must protect customer data and not share without consent. (10) Penalties: selling counterfeit goods online - up to 5 years imprisonment and/or NPR 200,000 fine under ETA Section 47; consumer rights violations - fines under Consumer Protection Act up to NPR 500,000. (11) Jurisdiction: disputes involving e-commerce can be filed at the consumer's local District Court. (12) The Department of Commerce accepts online consumer complaints through its portal and toll-free number 1136.

title: OTT Platforms, Digital Streaming and Social Media Regulation
content: Over-the-Top (OTT) media services and digital streaming platforms in Nepal are regulated under the Telecommunications Act 2053, Electronic Transaction Act 2063, and the Directives on Social Media and OTT Services. Key regulations: (1) OTT platforms (Netflix, YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Viber, Discord) providing communication services must register with Nepal Telecommunications Authority (NTA). (2) Content regulation: OTT platforms must remove illegal content (hate speech, defamation, obscenity, copyright infringement) within 72 hours of receiving a valid complaint (ETA Section 47). (3) Social media platforms must have a grievance officer for Nepali users. (4) Streaming of pirated content is illegal under Copyright Act 2058. (5) Live streaming of illegal activities (gambling, violence, adult content) is prohibited. (6) Data localization: OTT platforms processing Nepali user data may be required to store data within Nepal (proposed Data Protection Bill). (7) Interception: Law enforcement can request user data from OTT platforms with court order under the Telecommunications Act Section 41. (8) Social media accounts of public figures and government bodies are considered public records. (9) Political advertising on social media must comply with Election Commission guidelines. (10) Misinformation and disinformation on OTT platforms: platforms must implement fact-checking mechanisms. (11) ISP-level blocking: NTA can direct ISPs to block content or platforms that violate Nepali law. (12) VPN usage: not illegal per se but using VPN to access blocked content or commit crimes is illegal. (13) Telecom Service Providers cannot throttle or block legitimate OTT services without NTA approval.
